BUSS1020 Week 10

BUSS1020 Week 10 — Welch, Paired and Two-Proportion Inference

Selecting a design

Independent groups require independent-sample methods. Randomly assigning 50 people to two training groups of 25 produces independent groups; measuring the same 50 people before and after training produces paired observations. Different people can also be dependent when deliberately matched. The study design determines the method.

Paired samples measure the same units twice, such as company profits before and after a tax change. Matched samples pair distinct units by relevant characteristics, such as test markets matched on population size or demographics. Both are analysed through within-pair differences.

For independent mean comparisons, pooling estimates a common population variance; Welch's method does not assume equal population variances. A rough diagnostic is max(s₁,s₂)/min(s₁,s₂) < 2, where s₁ and s₂ are sample standard deviations. It can motivate an equal-variance assumption but does not prove it. A preliminary variance test is not required to use Welch's method.

Notation and independent-sample uncertainty

For group j = 1 or 2, nⱼ is sample size, x̄ⱼ is sample mean, sⱼ is sample standard deviation, and μⱼ is population mean. The parameter is μ₁ − μ₂; its unbiased estimator is x̄₁ − x̄₂. Let Δ₀ denote the hypothesised difference, usually zero.

For independent samples, Var(X̄₁ − X̄₂) = σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂. Independence sets covariance to zero, so variances add. Normal populations give exact normal sampling distributions for the means; a Central Limit Theorem approximation requires adequate sample sizes and finite variances.

Welch's separate-variance t method

Welch's method assumes random independent samples, with normal populations or sufficiently well-behaved large-sample mean distributions. Practical guidelines are both samples at least 30, or both at least 15 for reasonably symmetric populations. It does not assume equal population variances.

SE = √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).

t = [(x̄₁ − x̄₂) − Δ₀]/SE.

The approximate Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom are:

ν = (s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂)² / {[(s₁²/n₁)²/(n₁ − 1)] + [(s₂²/n₂)²/(n₂ − 1)]}.

ν is data-dependent and usually noninteger. Excel t-distribution functions truncate a noninteger degrees-of-freedom input; software retaining fractional ν can produce a slightly different result. Using min(n₁ − 1,n₂ − 1) is a conservative alternative with a larger critical value and wider interval.

A two-sided 1 − α confidence interval is:

(x̄₁ − x̄₂) ± t*SE, where t* is the positive 1 − α/2 t percentile with ν degrees of freedom.

The numerator and decision logic are shared. With equal sample sizes and similar variances, results tend to be similar. With strongly unequal sample sizes and variances, differences can be important.

Example 1 — Amazon sales-generation experiment

Users are randomly assigned to two methods. Method 1 uses expert raters and prominent authors' ratings and reviews; method 2 uses buyer reviews and data analysis. Group summaries are:

Test H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0 against H₁: μ₁ − μ₂ ≠ 0 at α = 0.05.

s₁²/n₁ = 28.5156/120 = 0.23763.

s₂²/n₂ = 71.5716/125 = 0.57257.

SE = √0.81020 = 0.9001.

t = (23.10 − 45.52)/0.9001 ≈ −24.91.

ν = 0.81020²/[0.23763²/119 + 0.57257²/124] ≈ 210.5.

The positive two-sided critical magnitude is about 1.9713. Reject H₀ because |t| is far larger.

The p-value is extremely small, not mathematically zero. The 95% interval is −22.42 ± 1.9713(0.90), approximately −$24.19 to −$20.65 per year. Method 2 has a higher estimated population mean purchase amount; the subtraction order explains the negative difference.

Example 2 — NYSE and NASDAQ under Welch's method

Use n₁ = 21, x̄₁ = 3.27%, s₁ = 1.30 percentage points, n₂ = 25, x̄₂ = 2.53%, and s₂ = 1.16 percentage points. The observed difference is 0.74 percentage points.

SE = √(1.30²/21 + 1.16²/25) ≈ 0.36645.

t = 0.74/SE = 2.0193, with ν = 40.5744, approximately 40.6. The two-sided p-value is near 0.0501, giving non-rejection at 5%. The standard-deviation ratio is 1.30/1.16 = 1.121. If equal variances are assumed instead, sₚ² = 1.502145, t ≈ 2.040 and p ≈ 0.047, giving rejection. Borderline decisions require the specified method and unrounded probabilities.

Example 3 — FoodPlace Real Citrus Cola placement

Ten stores with beverage-area placement have mean 50.3 and sample SD 18.73; ten with produce-area placement have mean 72 and SD 12.54. Test a zero mean difference with Welch's method.

SE = √(18.73²/10 + 12.54²/10) = √(35.08129 + 15.72516) ≈ 7.128.

t = (50.3 − 72)/SE ≈ −3.04455. Using integer df = 16, the two-sided p-value is 0.007726 and the 5% critical values are ±2.119905. Reject equal means. The small groups require a defensible population-shape assumption.

Paired-difference inference

For pair i, define Dᵢ = X₁ᵢ − X₂ᵢ. There are n pairs, not 2n independent observations. Let μ_D be the population mean difference, D̄ = ΣDᵢ/n the sample mean difference and s_D = √[Σ(Dᵢ − D̄)²/(n − 1)] the sample difference standard deviation.

For H₀: μ_D = Δ₀:

t = (D̄ − Δ₀)/(s_D/√n), with df = n − 1.

A two-sided interval is D̄ ± t*s_D/√n, using the positive 1 − α/2 percentile. Upper-tail rejection is t > t*; lower-tail rejection is t < −t*; two-sided rejection is |t| > t*, with the critical percentile chosen for the relevant number of tails.

Differences must be randomly and independently sampled across pairs. Exact small-sample inference assumes normally distributed differences; sufficiently large samples of differences support approximation, with n > 30 a practical guideline. Symmetry can support smaller-sample approximations, but the condition applies to differences rather than separately to each measurement column.

Pairing can reduce between-unit noise and improve power when measurements within pairs are positively related. The direction of H₁ depends on how D is defined. Reversing D reverses its mean and statistic, but not the substantive answer when the alternative is also reversed.

ΣDᵢ = 21, so D̄ = 21/5 = 4.2.

Squared deviations sum to 4.84 + 96.04 + 10.24 + 17.64 + 0.04 = 128.8.

s_D² = 128.8/4 = 32.2, so s_D = 5.6745.

SE = 5.6745/√5 = 2.5377.

For H₀: μ_D = 0 against H₁: μ_D > 0, t = 4.2/2.5377 = 1.655 with df = 4.

At α = 0.05, the upper critical value is 2.1318, approximately 2.132. The one-sided p-value is 0.0866.

Fail to reject: there is insufficient evidence that training reduces complaints. Only five pairs are available, so approximate normality of differences is an important assumption.

Alternatively, D = After − Before gives differences (−2,−14,−1,0,−4), D̄ = −4.2 and t = −1.655. Test H₁: μ_D < 0 against lower critical value −2.1318; the p-value and conclusion are unchanged.

For a two-sided question about any change, the critical magnitude is 2.7764, p ≈ 0.1733, and the 95% interval for Before − After is −2.85 to 11.25 complaints. Its inclusion of zero agrees with non-rejection for that two-sided question.

Two population proportions

For independent groups, Xⱼ is the success count, nⱼ sample size, πⱼ population proportion and pⱼ = Xⱼ/nⱼ sample proportion. The parameter is π₁ − π₂, estimated without bias by p₁ − p₂.

For H₀: π₁ = π₂, estimate the common proportion with:

p̄ = (X₁ + X₂)/(n₁ + n₂).

This is a sample-size-weighted proportion, not generally the simple average of p₁ and p₂. The equality-null statistic is:

z = (p₁ − p₂)/√[p̄(1 − p̄)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)].

Use the approximate standard normal distribution, not Student t. Approximation requires adequate successes and failures in both groups; inspect n₁p₁, n₁(1 − p₁), n₂p₂ and n₂(1 − p₂), with all at least 5 as a practical guideline. Null-based expected counts also inform adequacy for the equality test.

A 1 − α confidence interval does not assume equality and uses separate estimates:

(p₁ − p₂) ± z√[p₁(1 − p₁)/n₁ + p₂(1 − p₂)/n₂].*

Here z* is the 1 − α/2 normal percentile. This unpooled Wald interval is not an exact algebraic inversion of the pooled equality test. A difference can legitimately be negative; its parameter space is [−1,1], not [0,1].

For a specified nonzero null difference Δ₀, an approximate unpooled Wald statistic is:

z = [(p₁ − p₂) − Δ₀]/√[p₁(1 − p₁)/n₁ + p₂(1 − p₂)/n₂].

Do not use equality-null pooling for a nonzero difference. This is a large-sample approximation, not an assertion of exact finite-sample calibration.

Example 6 — Referendum voting intentions

Among 72 sampled men, 36 intend to vote Yes; among 50 sampled women, 35 intend to vote Yes. Test equal population proportions against a two-sided alternative at α = 0.05.

p₁ = 36/72 = 0.50 and p₂ = 35/50 = 0.70.

p̄ = (36 + 35)/(72 + 50) = 71/122 ≈ 0.582, not 0.60.

Pooled SE = √[0.582(0.418)(1/72 + 1/50)] ≈ 0.09080.

z = (0.50 − 0.70)/0.09080 ≈ −2.20.

|z| > 1.96; the two-sided p-value is approximately 0.0276, or 0.028 to three decimals. Reject equal proportions.

The four observed counts are 36 successes and 36 failures for men, and 35 successes and 15 failures for women; all exceed the guideline. The unpooled SE is √[0.50(0.50)/72 + 0.70(0.30)/50] = 0.08759. The 95% interval is −0.20 ± 1.96(0.08759), or −0.372 to −0.028. It estimates a male Yes proportion about 2.8 to 37.2 percentage points below the female proportion.

Covariance and correlation

Covariance measures joint variation: the sample covariance is s₁₂ = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ)/(n − 1) for n paired observations. The sample correlation is r = s₁₂/(sₓsᵧ), where sₓ and sᵧ are the two sample standard deviations. Correlation is unitless and lies from −1 to 1; covariance depends on measurement units. Independence implies zero covariance when the relevant moments exist, but zero covariance does not generally imply independence.

Excel implementation

Use Data → Data Analysis after enabling Analysis ToolPak. Select t-Test: Two-Sample Assuming Unequal Variances, t-Test: Two-Sample Assuming Equal Variances, or t-Test: Paired Two Sample for Means according to the design. Specify data ranges, null difference and α.

• T.TEST(array1,array2,tails,3) uses unequal variances; type 2 pools variances; type 1 uses paired differences.

• T.INV.2T(alpha,df) returns a positive two-sided critical magnitude.

• T.DIST.2T(ABS(t),df) returns a two-sided t p-value.

• For a proportion statistic, 2*NORM.S.DIST(-ABS(z),TRUE) returns the two-sided normal p-value.

• A lower-tail normal p-value is NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE); an upper-tail value is 1-NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE).

For appreciable sampling fractions without replacement, a finite-population standard-error correction requires the relevant population size for each group. The factor is √[(N − n)/(N − 1)] for a simple random sample of n from N; it is commonly considered when n/N > 0.05.
